## Chosen hook

Line 1 (Contrarian, aimed at the instrument people are reaching for, never at the GP or the lab):

"There is a thing men do now with a blood test result. They photograph the printout, paste it into a chatbot, and ask a machine that has never met them what it means."

Re-hook: "I understand the reflex completely. The number arrived with no translation."

## Script

**Emotion:** Recognition, with credibility underneath.

> There is a thing men do now with a blood test result. They photograph the printout, paste it into a chatbot, and ask a machine that has never met them what it means.
>
> I understand the reflex completely. The number arrived with no translation.
>
> The appointment ended with "all normal" and a hand on the door. Or the private panel sent back a wall of figures and a green tick. Either way nobody read it back to you in plain English, so you went looking for someone who would.
>
> Here is the part worth knowing before you paste anything anywhere. Every line on that sheet is telling you the same four things.
>
> The marker, which is what was measured. The value, which is your number on the day. The units, which are the scale it was measured on. And the reference range, which is the band the lab calls normal.
>
> The fourth one quietly runs the whole show, and it is the one most people read wrong. A reference range is not a health target. It is a statistical band. The lab tests a large group of people it considers healthy and draws the range to cover about 19 in 20 of them. Which means, by design, one in twenty perfectly healthy people sit outside it.
>
> So the range answers one question. Is this person outside what we would expect for the population. It was never built to answer the other one. Is this person well, and performing the way they want to be.
>
> Two different questions. Most men reading their results are asking the second one.
>
> None of that is the lab getting it wrong, and it is not your GP getting it wrong either. The range is doing the job it was built for. It just is not the job you needed doing at 11pm with a printout in your hand.
>
> That gap is why I am building Andro Prime.
>
> If you have a set of results sitting in the NHS App or a drawer right now, which of those four things did you actually read?

**First comment:** I am building Andro Prime, plain-English men's health read from your blood. The longer version of this, including the units, the timing rule that catches men out on testosterone, and when a result is a GP conversation rather than ours, is here: https://andro-prime.com/blog/how-to-read-blood-test-results?utm_source=linkedin

## Craft notes

- **Archetype:** Contrarian, the LinkedIn default per `written-post-playbook.md`. The wedge is aimed at the reference range and at the instrument men are reaching for, never at the GP and never at the lab. The paragraph beginning "None of that is the lab getting it wrong" is load-bearing rather than padding: `avatar-mark.md` §C records that mainstream anti-clinician anger is really billing distrust, so an anti-GP frame would misread the reader.
- **Structure choice, checked against the avatar rather than against ease of clearance.** The competing angle was the units section, which is the article's other strong standalone idea. It was rejected because its implicit ask is "go away and learn a conversion table", and Mark's defining problem is an excess of unassessed reading, not a shortage of it (`avatar-mark.md` §A, "read enough to be dangerous and not enough to be sure", and the Tier 2 interpretation gap). The four-things frame gives him something to apply to a sheet he already owns, in one pass, tonight.
- **The chatbot opening is the avatar's own behaviour, not a swipe at him.** The Tier 2 wrong-tool pair in `avatar-mark.md` is explicit that the instinct is right and the instrument is wrong, and that the behaviour must never be mocked. The post says "I understand the reflex completely" in the second line for exactly that reason.
- **Device 7 (understatement at the peak):** "Two different questions. Most men reading their results are asking the second one." Shortest paragraph in the post, doing the most work.
- **No personal history and no bloodwork figure.** The only first-person claims are a statement of understanding and a statement about the business, both true of Keith. Nothing here needs a filed result or a ruling to stand up.
- **Deliberate distance from `2026-07-28-four-worth-seeing`.** That post ran the normal-range wedge as "an answer to a different question" and named four Kit 2 markers. This one shares the underlying idea and must not repeat its shape: it names no marker, teaches a reading habit instead of a panel, and enters through the chatbot behaviour rather than through the "everything looks normal" conversation. Worth checking before scheduling that the two are not sitting adjacent in the calendar.

## Rails held

Written as an allowlist of what the copy does, never a list of what it avoids, because a note that spells out the red-flag terms puts them back into the scanned file.

The post stays on the education side of the line throughout. It describes how a reference interval is derived and what question it was built to answer, and it points its contrarian energy at that interval rather than at any clinician. It names no marker, no ingredient and no product, so the EFSA tables are not in play. It carries no bloodwork figure, so there is nothing to substantiate against a filed result. The founder is disclosed in the body, which the LinkedIn format expects. Certainty replaces guessing: the offer is a way to read a sheet, not an outcome. The CTA is a single soft link in the first comment, routed to the canonical article, which carries the test-selector CTA onward. No em dashes, no bullet lists in the post body, no engagement bait.
